hints: Compare the nuclei of the two large white cells - look at how many lobes each nucleus has and how dark and round it is.
Recall which phagocyte has a 3 to 5 lobed nucleus for squeezing through walls, and which larger mononuclear cell has a single kidney-shaped nucleus.
walkthrough:
Read the Nucleus Shape**
Cell X has granular cytoplasm and a dark nucleus divided into several connected lobes. That multilobed appearance is classic for a neutrophil and helps its flexible nucleus squeeze between endothelial cells.

Contrast With Cell Y**
Cell Y is larger with a single very large, dark, rounded to kidney-shaped nucleus filling most of the cell and little visible cytoplasm. That mononuclear appearance fits a monocyte, which later becomes a macrophage in tissues.
Final answer: X - neutrophil; Y - monocyte (accept B-lymphocyte / T-lymphocyte).

hints: Measure line Z on Fig. 3.1 in mm with a ruler, then convert that image size to micrometres to match the actual size units.
Remember the magnification triangle: magnification equals image size divided by actual size, with both in the same units.
walkthrough:
Measure Image and Convert Units**
Measure line Z on the printed image. It is about $12 \text{ mm}$. Since $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \, \mu\text{m}$, image size $I = 12 \times 1000 = 12000 \, \mu\text{m}$. Actual width $A = 8 \, \mu\text{m}$ is given.

Apply M = I / A**
Use $M = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}} = \frac{12000}{8} = 1500$. So magnification = x 1500. Magnification has no units because units cancel.
Final answer: formula: $M = \frac{I}{A}$; $I \approx 12 \text{ mm} = 12000 \, \mu\text{m}$, $A = 8 \, \mu\text{m}$, magnification = x 1500.

hints: Start where respiring tissues release lots of carbon dioxide - think what diffuses into the red blood cell and what enzyme waits inside.
Follow what carbon dioxide plus water becomes, and what that acid then splits into.
Think where the released hydrogen ions go - which protein picks them up inside the red cell.
Link that binding to a shape change in haemoglobin and what that means for the oxygen it is carrying.
walkthrough:
Make Acid From CO2**
At respiring tissues $CO_2$ diffuses into red blood cells. Inside, carbonic anhydrase speeds up $CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3$, carbonic acid. Without the enzyme this would be too slow to cope with tissue $CO_2$.

Release Hydrogen Ions**
Carbonic acid dissociates at once: $H_2CO_3 \rightarrow H^+ + HCO_3^-$. So a pulse of $H^+$ appears exactly where $CO_2$ is high, which is the signal that oxygen is needed.

Bind H+ to Haemoglobin**
The $H^+$ binds to haemoglobin, forming haemoglobinic acid. This is the Bohr effect. It is not that oxygen is pushed out on purpose, it is chemistry: $H^+$ changes ionic bonds in the globin chains.

Unload Oxygen**
Binding $H^+$ causes an allosteric change in tertiary and quaternary structure of oxyhaemoglobin, lowering its affinity for $O_2$. Oxygen is displaced and released, then diffuses out to respiring cells.

Final answer: Carbonic anhydrase catalyses $CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3$ (carbonic acid); $H_2CO_3$ dissociates to $H^+ + HCO_3^-$; $H^+$ binds to haemoglobin to form haemoglobinic acid; this causes allosteric change in tertiary structure releasing $O_2$ from oxyhaemoglobin.

hints: Recall where a competitive inhibitor binds and what happens when there is little substrate versus a lot of substrate to compete with it.
Think how that competition changes the early steep part of the curve and whether the final plateau can still be reached.
walkthrough:
Lower Rate at Low Substrate**
Sulfonamide is competitive, so it occupies the active site of carbonic anhydrase. At low substrate concentration it blocks many enzymes, so the initial rate is lower. Your curve must lie below the original curve.

Same Plateau at High Substrate**
At very high substrate concentration, substrate outcompetes the inhibitor for the active site, so Vmax is unchanged. Your curve rises more slowly then merges with the original line as both level off to the same plateau.

Final answer: Draw a second curve starting at origin below the original curve at low to intermediate substrate concentration, then converging to meet the original Vmax plateau at high substrate concentration.
